## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sūkarajātaka* (Ja 153), translated as *The Boar*, is a short canonical birth story preserved in the *Jātaka* section of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. The canonical verse opens with the incipit *Catuppado ’haṁ samma* ("You are a fourfoot") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related this discourse while residing at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, prompted by an aged elder (*aññataraṁ mahallakattheraṁ*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), an insolent boar challenges a lion to combat, only to cover himself in filth; when the lion disdains fighting him, the boars flee in fear that the lion will return to destroy them [Fausböll 1879]. In the formal identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the aged boar was the elderly monk of the present day, while the noble lion was the Buddha himself in a previous life [Fausböll 1879].

The text of the *Sūkarajātaka* and its commentary were edited in Roman script by V. Fausböll in the second volume of *The Jātaka together with its Commentary* (1879) [Fausböll 1879]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text across four languages [SuttaCentral].

Regarding parallels and textual reuse, SuttaCentral lists no parallels for this narrative in other canonical or extra-canonical collections [SuttaCentral]. Furthermore, automated textual analysis conducted by DharmaNexus indicates no Pali-internal text reuse and no cross-language matches with Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora meeting the threshold score of 10 [DharmaNexus].
